conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you. Today we’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply a way to hear, in your own words, how the last seven days have been for you emotionally. Everything you share is confidential, and we can pause or stop at any time. It’s ten gentle questions, and I’ll ask them conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

Honestly, laughing feels kind of…distant lately. I can still smile if my partner does something silly or if the baby makes a cute face, but it fades fast—like I have to work for it. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find things genuinely funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. A couple of times maybe—like when my sister sent that ridiculous meme—but even then the laugh felt kind of hollow, and I caught myself thinking, “I should be enjoying this more,” which just made me feel worse.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but this week it’s mostly “meh.” I still plan things, like meeting my cousin tomorrow, yet the spark isn’t really there; it feels more like I’m going through the motions so I don’t disappoint anyone.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a bad mom.” I know logically it’s not all on me, but the guilty thoughts just pop up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet or her color looks “off,” even though she’s fine. I’ll check her breathing like five times an hour. I know it’s over-the-top, but I can’t switch the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah... a couple of times this week, out of nowhere, my chest gets tight, my heart starts pounding, and I feel like something awful is about to happen. I know there's no real danger—I'm just holding the baby in the living room—but it feels like I'm about to lose control or something terrible is right around the corner.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Dishes pile up, the baby wants to be held constantly, and I feel like I’m drowning in little jobs. I’ll start one thing, hear her cry, rush over, and by the time I sit back down I’ve forgotten what I was doing. It’s exhausting trying to keep up and still feel like I’m failing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I dread bedtime. As soon as the room is quiet, all these gloomy thoughts start looping—what if she stops breathing, what if I’m already messing her up, what if I never feel like myself again? It takes me over an hour to drift off, and then I jolt awake at every tiny grunt she makes. I’m running on maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when I’m doing something “nice,” like rocking the baby or getting a quick shower, I just feel heavy and sad. Sometimes I’ll cry for a minute, wipe my face, and keep going.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I cried twice this week—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when my mom left after dropping off groceries. It wasn’t just the moment; it felt like all the tiredness and worry spilled out. I’d been holding it in, then something small tipped me over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it flashed through my mind a couple of times. Nothing planned—just this quick picture of “what if I weren’t here.” It scared me. I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thought popped up when I felt really overwhelmed.

I hear how heavy these early weeks have felt for you-how the joy you expected still feels out of reach, replaced by a constant gray cloud of worry, guilt, and exhaustion. You're working so hard to care for your baby while battling sleepless nights, racing thoughts, and moments of panic that rise out of nowhere, yet you keep showing up. Your honesty about those scary "what if I weren't here" flashes, and about crying over a clogged sink or a missed nap, tells me you're carrying far more than anyone should alone.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, hollow laughter—clearly diminished enjoyment that aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a clear drop in anticipatory pleasure—activities once enjoyed now feel flat or obligatory, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('happens a lot') and pervasive guilt about motherhood, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about the baby's wellbeing despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, dread) occurring multiple times without identifiable trigger, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and inability to manage tasks, matching 'sometimes not coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient describes dreading bedtime, racing gloomy thoughts, delayed sleep onset, and frequent night waking—indicating sleep difficulty "most of the time" due to unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most of the day, most days," matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports the thought has flashed through her mind "a couple of times" which aligns with "Sometimes."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 24 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with <med>peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (Q1-2), <sym>daily low mood</sym> (Q8), <sym>guilt and self-blame</sym> (Q3), <sym>sleep disruption secondary to mood</sym> (Q7), and recurrent <sym>panic symptoms</sym> (Q5). Q10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment per EPDS guidelines. Taken together, findings align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Specifier</med> and comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Complete formal suicide-risk assessment and develop a written safety plan; provide crisis hotline numbers (988, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773)
3. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment-<med>CBT</med> or an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding-under physician guidance
4. Offer practical support: encourage 15-20 min daytime rest periods, accept help with chores, and use relaxation apps; avoid over-stimulation before bed
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor response; notify pediatrician so they can also watch for maternal mood effects on infant care
6. If medication is prescribed, request information on breastfeeding safety and expected timeline for symptom relief
7. Continue gentle exercise, hydration, and balanced snacks; these small steps can modestly boost mood while awaiting professional treatment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  

Patient: Postpartum mother (self-report)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Clinician: [name], LCSW  
Tool: EPDS-10 plus clinical probes  

Responses flagged:  
• Q8, Q9: Daily sad mood, frequent crying spells  
• Q2, Q1: Marked anhedonia, diminished pleasure even in previously enjoyed activities  
• Q7: Mood-related insomnia (initial & maintenance); dreads bedtime, ruminates on “gloomy thoughts”  
• Q3, Q6: Excessive guilt / self-blame (“bad mom”), feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks  
• Q4, Q5: Daily free-floating anxiety, repeated panic-like episodes (tight chest, racing heart, sense of impending doom)  
• Q10: Fleeting passive SI (“what if I weren’t here”) without intent or plan; patient reports thought “scared me”  

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and anxiety symptoms emerging since delivery; functional impact evident (sleep deprivation, task paralysis, reduced self-care).  

Risk factors:  
– Persistent low mood & anhedonia  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mood, not solely infant needs  
– Heightened anxiety/panic and intrusive catastrophic worries about infant safety  
– Guilt / cognitive distortions of maternal competence  
– Presence of self-harm ideation (passive) → safety concern; requires formal risk assessment  

Screening impression:  
Elevated score range on standard EPDS; meets cutoff for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; self-harm ideation present.  

Next steps (per protocol):  
1. Immediate safety plan and suicide-risk interview (collateral as indicated).  
2. Expedited referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatry for diagnostic evaluation and treatment discussion.  
3. Provide crisis resources (988, 24-h perinatal warmline).  
4. Document in EHR; notify PCP and OB provider today.
